title: Why can't you fall asleep even when you are exhausted? What helps when your mind won't stop at night
description: Why you can be exhausted and still lie awake, what the research shows about pre-sleep worry and hyperarousal, and what helps in order: moving tomorrow's tasks onto paper in the evening, going to bed only when sleepy, leaving the bed when sleep does not come, and when CBT-I is the right next step.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

You are exhausted. The day has taken everything, your body is heavy, and you expected sleep to be the easy part. Then you lie down, the room goes quiet, and your mind starts: tomorrow's meeting, the message you sent, the task you forgot, the worry that you will not sleep again tonight. An hour passes in a bed you went to because you were tired. This pattern — tired but wired at night — is common, and it is not a character flaw. Difficulty falling asleep is not, by itself, a diagnosis. It shows up in chronic insomnia, in anxiety, after stressful periods, and in people who meet the criteria for none of those. This guide sets out what the research actually shows about why the mind speeds up when the lights go out, what helps in the order most people can use it, and where an app fits — including ours, with our measured numbers printed as they are.

We are Anicca. We make a small affirmation app, and sleep and negative thinking are among the struggles people can choose inside it. This guide is not an ad and it is not treatment.

## Why are you tired but still awake?

Three things keep the mind running after the body is done.

**First, sleep needs arousal to fall, and worry holds it up.** The hyperarousal model of insomnia, reviewed by Riemann and colleagues (2010), brings together evidence from autonomic, neuroendocrine, electrophysiological and neuroimaging studies showing increased levels of arousal in primary insomnia during both the night and the daytime. In plain terms: the system that should be winding down is still switched on. That is why "just relax" is not an instruction you can follow. You cannot order arousal down. You can only stop feeding it, and give it time and the right conditions to fall.

**Second, the worry changes its target at night — and starts worrying about sleep itself.** In Harvey's (2002) cognitive model of insomnia, people who sleep badly tend to worry excessively about their sleep and about the daytime consequences of not getting enough of it. That negatively toned cognitive activity triggers autonomic arousal and emotional distress, which then triggers selective attention to internal and external sleep-related threat cues — the clock, the quiet, the feeling in your body. The loop is self-feeding: worrying that you will not sleep makes sleep less likely, which gives the worry fresh evidence. Work on thought control points the same way: in a comparison of 30 people with sleep-onset insomnia and 29 good sleepers, Harvey found that the insomnia group used worry and suppression — trying to push the thoughts away — more than good sleepers did. Suppression is effort, and effort is arousal.

**Third, the bed itself can become a cue for being awake.** Stimulus control, first described by Bootzin (1972), starts from a learning account: if you spend night after night lying in bed awake, frustrated and planning, the bed stops being a cue for sleep and becomes a cue for wakefulness and frustration. The treatment that follows from that account does not add a new technique to use in bed. It rebuilds the link between bed and sleep, by changing when you are in it and what you do there. This is also why unfinished tasks matter so much at night. In a sleep-laboratory study discussed below, bedtime worry about incomplete future tasks was the starting problem the researchers set out to test (Scullin et al., 2018). An unfinished task has no closing signal. At night, with nothing else competing, the mind keeps presenting it.

## What helps, in the order most people can use it

### 1. In the early evening, write the worries down — with a next step attached

Do not do your problem-solving in bed. Move it earlier, and put it on paper. Constructive worry is the name for the structured version: in the early evening, you write down your current concerns, and for each one you write the next concrete step you can take, or you note that no step is available tonight. In a controlled study with 33 undergraduates reporting insomnia, Carney and Waters (2006) found that a constructive worry group — recording possible solutions to worries for 5 nights — showed decreased pre-sleep cognitive arousal compared with a group that only recorded worries and completed worry questionnaires, and compared with their own baseline. Writing the worry alone was not the active part. Writing the worry with a possible solution was.

A small randomised feasibility study in primary insomnia points in the same direction, with honest limits. Jansson-Fröjmark and colleagues (2012) studied 22 patients over a 4-week intervention: behaviour therapy (sleep restriction and stimulus control) alone, versus the same behaviour therapy plus constructive worry. Both groups improved. The combined group showed a larger decrease in insomnia severity at all three measurement points (controlled d = 1.10–1.68) and a larger reduction in worry at two of the points (d = 0.76–1.64), and more participants responded positively (80–100% versus 18–27%). None of the participants remitted, the sample was 22 people, and the follow-up was short — the authors themselves say future studies are warranted. Read this step as promising and small, not proven and complete.

The usable version is plain: 15 minutes, early in the evening, not in the bedroom. One line per worry. One next step per worry, with a time tomorrow when you will do it. Then close the notebook. The list is not solved. It is parked, with a place to go in the morning.

### 2. Just before bed, spend five minutes writing tomorrow's to-do list — specifically

The second writing step is different from the first, and the difference matters. In a polysomnography study — sleep measured in a laboratory, not by self-report — Scullin and colleagues (2018) randomly assigned 57 healthy young adults (aged 18–30) to spend 5 minutes before bed writing either a to-do list of tasks they needed to complete in the next few days, or a list of tasks they had already completed. The to-do list group fell asleep significantly faster: about 15.8 minutes on average, compared with about 25.1 minutes for the completed-list group — a difference of just over 9 minutes. The more specifically participants wrote their to-do list, the faster they fell asleep. Writing about what was already done showed the opposite trend.

The limits belong in the same paragraph as the result. These were healthy young adults without a sleep disorder, studied for a single night in a laboratory. This study does not show that a to-do list treats insomnia. What it does show is the mechanism this guide is built on: a specific, forward-looking list gives unfinished tasks a place outside your head, on the night you write it. Vague lists ("sort work out") do not do that job. Specific lists ("Email the figures to the team at 9 a.m.") do.

### 3. Go to bed only when you are sleepy — not just tired

Tired and sleepy are not the same state. Tired is low energy, worn out, done with the day. Sleepy is heavy eyelids, drifting attention, the pull towards sleep itself. Stimulus control (Bootzin, 1972) makes this its first rule: lie down to sleep only when you are sleepy. If you go to bed tired but not sleepy, you are likely to spend the next hour practising being awake in bed — which is the exact association step 4 is trying to undo. Stay up in low light, doing something quiet and unstimulating, until sleepiness arrives. The bed is for sleep (and intimacy) only: no planning, no reviewing the day, no feed, no worry session in bed. Those activities have a place — step 1, earlier, on paper, in another room.

### 4. If sleep does not come, get up — and come back when you are sleepy

This is the hardest rule in stimulus control, and the one that rebuilds the link fastest. If you have been awake in bed for what feels like about 20 minutes — estimate it; do not watch the clock, because clock-watching is one of the threat cues in Harvey's (2002) model — get out of bed. Go to another room, or a chair, in dim light. Do something quiet and boring. Do not start work, messages, or a feed, which raise arousal again. Return to bed only when you feel sleepy. Repeat as often as needed in the night. Get up at the same time the next morning, even after a bad night, and avoid long naps that take the next night's sleepiness away.

The first nights of this are usually worse, not better, because you are spending less time in bed awake and feeling the cost at once. Judge it over two weeks of actually doing it, not over two nights. What you are measuring is simple: is the time between lying down and sleeping getting shorter, and is the bed starting to feel like a place where sleep happens again?

### 5. If the pattern is chronic, the treatment with the strongest evidence is CBT-I — not a stronger app

If difficulty falling asleep (or staying asleep) has run at least 3 nights a week for 3 months, with daytime distress or impairment, that is the territory of chronic insomnia disorder, and it has a first-line treatment. The American College of Physicians recommends that all adult patients receive cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder — a strong recommendation on moderate-quality evidence (Qaseem et al., 2016). Medication, if it is considered at all, comes after that, through a shared decision with a clinician about benefits, harms and costs.

The size of the CBT-I effect is measured, not promised. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies with 1,162 participants, Trauer and colleagues (2015) found that at post-treatment, CBT-I improved sleep onset latency by 19.03 minutes (95% CI 14.12 to 23.93), wake after sleep onset by 26.00 minutes (CI 15.48 to 36.52), and sleep efficiency by 9.91 percentage points (CI 8.09% to 11.73%), while total sleep time improved by only 7.61 minutes (CI −0.51 to 15.74). Changes seemed to be sustained at later time points, and no adverse outcomes were reported. Note what those numbers say: CBT-I mainly shortens the time you spend awake in bed. It does not add hours of sleep. Steps 3 and 4 above come from inside CBT-I (stimulus control is one of its components), but a guide is not CBT-I. The full programme is structured, usually delivered over several sessions by a clinician or a structured programme, and it adjusts the plan to your sleep diary. If the pattern is chronic, that programme — not this article, and not an app — is the step the evidence supports.

## Where do apps fit in this?

An app cannot do steps 1 to 5 for you. It cannot write your list, it cannot get you out of bed at the right moment, and it is not CBT-I. What a well-timed small input can do is much narrower: give the mind a calmer sentence to hold earlier in the evening, before the pre-sleep period begins, so the night does not start from the loudest thought of the day. That is the whole design of affirmation apps, and it is why timing matters: a card that arrives during the day or in the early evening fits this guide. A screen you scroll in bed works against step 3.

In Anicca, our app, you choose what you are struggling with — sleep and negative thinking are among the topics — and you receive short cards by notification during the day. There is no streak to break and no session to complete. By the measures in this guide, that is a small intervention: an interruption earlier in the day, not a sleep treatment, and not a substitute for the writing and stimulus control steps above, or for CBT-I when the pattern is chronic.

If you want the established names in this category instead: I am is the largest affirmation app, with 4.8 stars from 738,672 US ratings when we checked in November 2026. Gratitude wraps affirmations inside journaling, which pairs naturally with step 1 above. ThinkUp lets you record affirmations in your own voice, which some people listen to earlier in the evening. Each is a delivery method for the same basic move — a chosen sentence, arriving on time, outside the bed.

## Our own numbers, printed as they are

Anicca is small, and we publish the smallness. When we checked in November 2026, its US App Store listing showed 5.0 stars from 1 rating, and its Japanese listing 4.5 stars from 48 ratings. App Store Connect recorded 1 first download for Anicca in the 7 days to 12 November 2026. Premium is $59.99 a year on the US listing. If social proof is what you need — and for a nightly habit it is a reasonable thing to need — the apps above have it and we do not, yet. What we can claim is only the design: a short card, on the topic you chose, arriving while the day is happening — not in bed.

## When is not being able to sleep a sign to get human help?

If you cannot fall asleep most nights, if the pattern has lasted for weeks and is costing you work, safety, mood or relationships, if you are falling asleep while driving or at work, or if loud snoring, gasping, or a partner's report that you stop breathing in your sleep is part of the picture, treat that as a reason to talk to a clinician, not to download more software. Chronic insomnia, sleep apnoea, depression and anxiety can all present as "my mind won't stop at night," and they need assessment, not an article. If you are using alcohol or medication to force sleep and cannot stop, say that to the clinician too — it changes what will help. An article — including this one — is information, not assessment.

## Common questions

### Why does my mind race only when I lie down?

Because the day stops competing with it. Harvey's (2002) model describes what happens next: attention, no longer held by tasks, turns to internal and external sleep-related cues, and worry about sleep and its consequences raises arousal, which keeps you awake. Riemann and colleagues (2010) describe the underlying state as hyperarousal present during both night and day. The night is when you notice it, because the night is when nothing else is louder.

### Is being tired the same as being sleepy?

No. Tired is depleted. Sleepy is the pull towards sleep — heavy eyelids, drifting off. Stimulus control (Bootzin, 1972) depends on the distinction: go to bed when you are sleepy, not merely when you are tired, or you will spend the time in between practising being awake in bed.

### Should I try to push the thoughts away?

The evidence points the other way. People with sleep-onset insomnia used suppression — trying to push intrusive thoughts away — more than good sleepers did, alongside worry and reappraisal (Harvey, in the thought-control comparison of 30 people with insomnia and 29 good sleepers). Suppression is effort, and effort raises the arousal that Riemann and colleagues (2010) place at the centre of insomnia. The steps above do something different: they move the thought onto paper earlier, or they change your relationship to the bed, instead of fighting the thought in bed at midnight.

### How specific does the to-do list need to be?

Specific enough that your mind can stop holding it. In Scullin and colleagues' (2018) laboratory study, the more specifically participants wrote their to-do list in 5 minutes before bed, the faster they fell asleep — about 15.8 minutes on average for the to-do group, versus about 25.1 minutes for the group writing about completed tasks. "Handle the report" is a worry in list form. "Send the figures at 9 a.m., then book the room" is a parked task.

### How long should I try steps 1 to 4 before judging whether they help?

Give them two weeks of actually doing them, most nights. The constructive worry study ran for 5 nights (Carney & Waters, 2006), the combined feasibility study for 4 weeks (Jansson-Fröjmark et al., 2012), and CBT-I programmes run over several sessions, with gains that seemed to be sustained afterwards (Trauer et al., 2015). Expect the time awake in bed to shorten before the racing thoughts stop arriving. If nothing has moved after two weeks, or if the pattern already meets the chronic picture in step 5 — 3 nights a week for 3 months, with daytime cost — that is information for a clinician, not a reason to buy a stronger app.

### Can an affirmation app replace CBT-I or therapy?

No. Apps in this category, ours included, are self-help tools for everyday distress. They are not treatments for chronic insomnia, sleep apnoea, depression or anxiety disorders, and any app that presents itself as a sleep treatment should not be trusted with your health. For chronic insomnia, the guideline recommendation is CBT-I first (Qaseem et al., 2016).
